questions.statement: Choose the structure that forms the third conditional.
questions.context: A student reviews the grammar chart before the English exam.

options.text: If + past perfect, would have + past participle
options.feedback: Right: the third conditional puts the past perfect in the if-clause and would have plus a past participle in the result.

options.text: If + present simple, will + infinitive
options.feedback: That pattern is the first conditional, which talks about a real future possibility, not an unreal past.

options.text: If + past simple, would + infinitive
options.feedback: That pattern is the second conditional, used for present or future hypotheticals, not for finished past situations.

options.text: If + past perfect, will have + past participle
options.feedback: The result clause of the third conditional uses would, not will, because the past situation never happened.

questions.explanation:
The third conditional describes an unreal past: the if-clause takes the past perfect and the result takes would have plus a past participle.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the sentence that is a third conditional.
questions.context: Maria checks her homework about unreal past situations.

options.text: If we leave earlier, we will catch the train.
options.feedback: That sentence is a first conditional about a real future chance, so it cannot describe an unreal past.

options.text: If we had left earlier, we would have caught the train.
options.feedback: Right: the past perfect in the if-clause and would have caught in the result make it a complete third conditional.

options.text: If we left earlier, we would catch the train.
options.feedback: That sentence is a second conditional, which imagines a present or future possibility instead.

options.text: If we had left earlier, we would catch the train.
options.feedback: Pairing the past perfect with would catch shifts the result to the present, so the sentence is mixed, not third.

questions.explanation:
A third conditional shows that a past action did not happen, pairing the past perfect with would have plus a past participle.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the meaning that the third conditional expresses.
questions.context: A tutor explains why the past perfect appears in conditional sentences.

options.text: A likely future situation that may still happen
options.feedback: Wrong: a likely future belongs to the first conditional, which still has a real chance of coming true.

options.text: A general truth that is always valid
options.feedback: Wrong: general truths use the zero conditional, with present simple in both clauses.

options.text: A hypothetical past situation that did not happen
options.feedback: Right: it imagines the opposite of what really happened, and the chance to change it is already gone.

options.text: A polite request about the present moment
options.feedback: Wrong: polite requests use would with a present idea, not the past perfect of this conditional.

questions.explanation:
The third conditional looks back at a past event that never occurred and imagines how the outcome would have changed.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Read 'If I had prepared better, I would be working there now' and choose why it is a mixed conditional.
questions.context: Diego rereads a sentence about a job interview that went badly.

options.text: The present condition has a result in the past
options.feedback: The order is the opposite: the if-clause is past and the result clause is present.

options.text: Both clauses refer to the same past moment
options.feedback: If both clauses referred to the past, the result would be would have been working, which is a third conditional.

options.text: The sentence uses the past perfect in both clauses
options.feedback: Only the if-clause uses the past perfect; the result uses would be, which points to now.

options.text: The past condition has a result in the present
options.feedback: Right: the missed preparation is finished, but the consequence of working there continues today.

questions.explanation:
Mixed conditionals cross time frames: a finished past cause can produce a result that is still true in the present.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Complete: If she had set an alarm, she ___ the exam.
questions.context: Laura missed the exam because she overslept that morning.

options.text: would not have missed
options.feedback: Right: the unreal past result needs would plus have plus the past participle missed.

options.text: will not miss
options.feedback: Wrong: will belongs to the first conditional, which describes real futures, not impossible pasts.

options.text: would not miss
options.feedback: Wrong: would not miss points to a present result, which would turn the sentence into a mixed one.

options.text: had not missed
options.feedback: Wrong: the if-clause already carries the past perfect, so the result clause cannot repeat that form.

questions.explanation:
After a past perfect if-clause, the result clause takes would have plus the past participle to complete the pattern.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Complete: If I had been more careful, I ___ my wallet.
questions.context: Pablo is telling his friend about the wallet he lost on Monday.

options.text: did not lose
options.feedback: Wrong: the past simple states a real past fact, but the sentence imagines an unreal one.

options.text: would not have lost
options.feedback: Right: would not have plus the past participle lost finishes the unreal past result correctly.

options.text: had not lost
options.feedback: Wrong: the past perfect belongs in the if-clause, not in the result clause of the conditional.

options.text: would not have lose
options.feedback: Wrong: after would have, the verb takes the past participle lost, not the bare form lose.

questions.explanation:
The result clause of a third conditional always pairs would have with the past participle of the main verb.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Complete the mixed conditional: If she had accepted the offer, she ___ in Ireland now.
questions.context: Elena refused an offer to study abroad two years ago.

options.text: would have studied
options.feedback: Wrong: would have studied keeps the whole sentence in the past, which contradicts the word now.

options.text: will be studying
options.feedback: Wrong: will is impossible here, because the condition is unreal and already finished.

options.text: would be studying
options.feedback: Right: the time marker now pulls the result into the present, so the sentence needs would be studying.

options.text: would have been studying
options.feedback: Wrong: would have been studying describes an unreal past action, not a present state.

questions.explanation:
When a past condition leads to a present result, the result clause uses would plus the base verb, as in would be studying.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Complete: The team ___ if the captain had taken the last shot.
questions.context: The basketball team reviews the final seconds of the match.

options.text: had won
options.feedback: Wrong: had won repeats the past perfect, which belongs only in the if-clause of a third conditional.

options.text: will win
options.feedback: Wrong: will win describes a real future outcome, but the shot is already history.

options.text: would win
options.feedback: Wrong: would win without have points to a present hypothetical, not to the finished match.

options.text: would have won
options.feedback: Right: the if-clause has the past perfect, so the result clause must take would have won.

questions.explanation:
A past perfect in the if-clause signals that the result clause needs would have plus a past participle.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Complete: If she were braver, she ___ swimming last summer.
questions.context: Sofia regrets never learning to swim as a child.

options.text: would have tried
options.feedback: Right: a present condition with a past result takes would have tried, a classic mixed pattern.

options.text: would try
options.feedback: Wrong: would try keeps the result in the present, but last summer fixes the action in the past.

options.text: had tried
options.feedback: Wrong: the past perfect cannot appear in the result clause of a conditional sentence.

options.text: will have tried
options.feedback: Wrong: will has no place here, because the condition is unreal rather than a prediction.

questions.explanation:
This mixed type starts with a present unreal condition and reaches back into the past with would have plus a participle.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the sentence that expresses regret about the past most appropriately.
questions.context: Ana writes an apology to a customer after a booking mistake.

options.text: If we check the dates, we will not charge you twice.
options.feedback: Wrong: this first conditional treats the double charge as a future possibility, ignoring what already happened.

options.text: If we had checked the dates, we would not have charged you twice.
options.feedback: Right: the past perfect and would not have charged present the mistake as finished, which fits an apology.

options.text: If we checked the dates, we would not charge you twice.
options.feedback: Wrong: the second conditional sounds hypothetical about now, but the customer was already overcharged.

options.text: If we had checked the dates, we will not charge you twice.
options.feedback: Wrong: pairing the past perfect with will is ungrammatical, because the clauses clash without a mixed meaning.

questions.explanation:
Apologies for past mistakes use the third conditional, because the harm is already done and only the hypothesis remains.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the sentence that is grammatically correct.
questions.context: A teacher marks the most common mistakes from the writing task.

options.text: If they would have rehearsed more, they would have performed better.
options.feedback: Wrong: would have must never enter the if-clause; the condition keeps the past perfect had rehearsed.

options.text: If they had rehearsed more, they had performed better.
options.feedback: Wrong: the result clause needs would have performed, because the past perfect alone cannot carry the hypothesis.

options.text: If they had rehearsed more, they would have performed better.
options.feedback: Right: it keeps the past perfect in the if-clause and would have performed in the result, the exact third pattern.

options.text: If they rehearsed more, they would have performed better.
options.feedback: Wrong: the past simple rehearsed belongs to the second conditional, so it clashes with the past result.

questions.explanation:
A correct third conditional reserves would have for the result clause and keeps the past perfect in the if-clause only.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Read 'If you would have told me, I would have helped' and identify the main error in it.
questions.context: During revision, a classmate questions one of the sentences on the board.

options.text: The result clause wrongly uses would have
options.feedback: Wrong: the result clause is fine, because would have helped is exactly what the third conditional requires.

options.text: The past perfect is missing from the result clause
options.feedback: Wrong: the result clause already contains the past participle helped after would have, so nothing is missing.

options.text: The sentence has no error at all
options.feedback: Wrong: the sentence holds a common learner error, because would have cannot introduce the condition.

options.text: The if-clause wrongly uses would have
options.feedback: Right: conditions never take would have, so the if-clause must read If you had told me instead.

questions.explanation:
Learners often copy would have into the if-clause, but the condition must stay in the past perfect: If you had told me.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the sentence that is a mixed conditional.
questions.context: A student compares conditional types in an essay about career choices.

options.text: If I had studied medicine, I would be a doctor today.
options.feedback: Right: the past condition is finished while the result would be holds today, which crosses time frames.

options.text: If I had studied medicine, I would have become a doctor.
options.feedback: Wrong: both clauses sit in the past, so this is a pure third conditional with no time shift.

options.text: If I studied medicine, I would become a doctor.
options.feedback: Wrong: both clauses sit in the present or future, which makes this a second conditional.

options.text: If I study medicine, I will become a doctor.
options.feedback: Wrong: both clauses sit in the real future, which makes this a first conditional.

questions.explanation:
A mixed conditional appears when one clause stays in the past and the other moves to the present, as in this pair.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the sentence that mixes a present condition with a past result.
questions.context: The class is correcting sentences that mix time references.

options.text: If he had not been so shy, he would have spoken at the meeting.
options.feedback: Wrong: both clauses look at the past, so this is a third conditional rather than a mixed one.

options.text: If he were not so shy, he would have spoken at the meeting.
options.feedback: Right: were not so shy describes his character now, while would have spoken points to the missed meeting.

options.text: If he were not so shy, he would speak at the meeting.
options.feedback: Wrong: both clauses describe the present, so this is a second conditional with no past result.

options.text: If he is not so shy, he will speak at the meeting.
options.feedback: Wrong: this is a first conditional about a real future chance, so no time mixing occurs.

questions.explanation:
The mixed pattern pairs a present unreal condition, were not so shy, with a past result, would have spoken at the meeting.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Read 'If you had listened to me, you would not be lost' and choose what the sentence implies.
questions.context: Two classmates argue about the meaning of one sentence.

options.text: You were lost then because you did not listen now
options.feedback: Wrong: the condition is in the past and the result in the present, not the other way round.

options.text: You listened, but you got lost anyway
options.feedback: Wrong: the third conditional always means the listener did not listen, since it imagines the unreal past.

options.text: You are lost now because you did not listen then
options.feedback: Right: the past fact did not listen explains the present state of being lost.

options.text: You will be lost unless you start listening
options.feedback: Wrong: the sentence describes a finished cause and a present effect, so nothing future is predicted.

questions.explanation:
With a mixed conditional, one sentence explains a present problem through its origin in a past decision.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the right correction of the sentence 'If the storm would have arrived later, the ships would have been saved'.
questions.context: A proofreader works through an article about a historical storm.

options.text: If the storm would arrive later, the ships would have been saved.
options.feedback: Wrong: would arrive leaves an illegal would in the condition and drops the past perfect entirely.

options.text: If the storm arrives later, the ships will be saved.
options.feedback: Wrong: this rewrites the event as a real future possibility, which erases the historical meaning.

options.text: If the storm had arrived later, the ships would be saved now.
options.feedback: Wrong: this version is grammatical, but adding now shifts the meaning to a mixed conditional.

options.text: If the storm had arrived later, the ships would have been saved.
options.feedback: Right: replacing would have arrived with had arrived fixes the if-clause and keeps the past meaning intact.

questions.explanation:
The proofreader only needs the past perfect in the condition; would have is reserved for the result clause.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the sentence that best expresses a lasting consequence of a past choice.
questions.context: A writer chooses the closing line of a scene full of regret.

options.text: If I had married Andreu, I would live by the sea now.
options.feedback: Right: the finished choice plus the present result would live now shows a consequence that still lasts.

options.text: If I marry Andreu, I will live by the sea.
options.feedback: Wrong: the first conditional treats the marriage as a real future option, which contradicts the regret.

options.text: If I married Andreu, I would live by the sea.
options.feedback: Wrong: the second conditional imagines a present choice that never existed, losing the past regret.

options.text: If I had married Andreu, I would have lived by the sea.
options.feedback: Wrong: the pure third conditional closes the story in the past, weakening the idea of a lasting effect.

questions.explanation:
Evaluating nuance: the mixed conditional keeps a past decision alive by projecting its effect into the present.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Draft A reads 'If we would have left sooner, we would not have missed the flight.' Choose the accurate evaluation of it.
questions.context: An editor judges two drafts of the same sentence about a missed flight.

options.text: It is correct because both clauses use would have
options.feedback: Wrong: matching would have in both clauses does not legitimize it, since the if-clause breaks the pattern.

options.text: It is incorrect because would have cannot appear in the if-clause
options.feedback: Right: the condition must use the past perfect, so the draft should read If we had left sooner.

options.text: It is incorrect because the result clause needs will not miss
options.feedback: Wrong: will not miss would describe a real future, but the flight was already missed.

options.text: It is correct in formal writing but wrong in speech
options.feedback: Wrong: the error is structural, not a matter of register, so it fails in speech and writing alike.

questions.explanation:
Evaluating a draft means checking the condition first: the past perfect belongs there, whatever the result does.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Read 'If the striker had seen the open player, he would have scored' and choose the line that contrasts would have scored with could have scored.
questions.context: A pundit debates the final minutes of the match with a colleague.

options.text: Both forms claim the result was merely possible
options.feedback: Wrong: would have does assert certainty about the unreal result, so the two forms are not the same.

options.text: Could have scored asserts certainty; would have scored asserts only possibility
options.feedback: Wrong: the modal meanings are swapped, because could expresses possibility and would expresses certainty.

options.text: Would have scored asserts certainty; could have scored asserts only possibility
options.feedback: Right: would have states the certain outcome, while could have only grants the chance to score.

options.text: Both forms claim the result was certain to happen
options.feedback: Wrong: could never asserts certainty, since it keeps the outcome open.

questions.explanation:
Modals change the strength of a third conditional result: would states the certain outcome and could states possibility.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Read 'If Napoleon had had better maps, history would be different' and choose the classification that keeps its meaning.
questions.context: A student writes the closing reflection for a history project.

options.text: It is a third conditional linking two past moments
options.feedback: Wrong: a third conditional would need would have been different, which fixes the result in the past.

options.text: It is a second conditional linking two present moments
options.feedback: Wrong: a second conditional needs a present condition, but the maps of the past cannot change.

options.text: It is ungrammatical because had had repeats the same word twice
options.feedback: Wrong: had had is correct, because the first had is the auxiliary and the second is the participle of have.

options.text: It is a mixed conditional linking a past cause to a present result
options.feedback: Right: the past condition had had better maps produces the result would be different, which holds in the present.

questions.explanation:
Classifying a sentence correctly depends on locating the time of each clause, not on counting repeated words.
---
